pr_title: drivers: usb_dc_mcux_ehci: fix endpoints index assignment
pr_body:
MCUX EHCI USB device controller supports a specific
number of bidirectional endpoints. Bidirectional means
that an endpoint object is represented to the outside
as an OUT and an IN Eindpoint with its own buffers
and control structures.

ep_abs_idx index refers to the corresponding control
structure, for example:

```
 EP addr | ep_idx | ep_abs_idx
-------------------------------
 0x00    | 0x00   | 0x00
 0x80    | 0x00   | 0x01
 0x01    | 0x01   | 0x02
 0x81    | 0x01   | 0x03
 ....    | ....   | ....
```

The NUM_OF_EP_MAX (and number of s_ep_ctrl) should be double
of num_bidir_endpoints. There is also no need to reserve
endpoint addresses for this controller type.

Fixes: #27569
Depends/associated with https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/hal_nxp/pull/54

issue_context.title: mimxrt1050_evk:samples.usb.cdc-acm-composite failed
issue_context.body:
Describe the bug
building samples/subsys/usb/cdc_acm_composite/ board, it would report a wrong.

To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

    west build -b mimxrt1050_evk samples/subsys/usb/cdc_acm_composite/
    west flash
    see error

Logs and console output
DEBUG   - DEVICE: *** Booting Zephyr OS build zephyr-v2.3.0-1774-g34859d0d3e40  ***
DEBUG   - DEVICE: [00:00:00.005,000] <err> usb_dc_mcux_ehci: Wrong endpoint index/address
DEBUG   - DEVICE: [00:00:00.005,000] <err> cdc_acm_composite: Failed to enable USB

Environment (please complete the following information):

    OS: Fedora28
    Toolchain: Zephyr-sdk-0.11.3
    Commit ID: 34859d0d3e
comments: Where things stopped working is with e0b2227c, but looking at the PR it appears to just add tests for `(ep_abs_idx >= NUM_OF_EP_MAX)` so I suspect the USB data structures always reported a value larger than NUM_OF_EP_MAX. So still digging.

@jfischer-phytec-iot, what I'm seeing is that the way the kinetis and mcux implementations of `usb_dc_ep_check_cap()` is doing a test on BIT(0) of the index value to determine if the endpoint can be an IN endpoint. The higher layer logic appears to be trying to put the IN endpoints at address 0x80 where the 0x80 bit mask indicates an IN endpoint. A macro extracts the true index value using:

n*2 + 1 (if the 0x80 bit is set)

This macro basically ensures that the IN endpoints will be on odd index boundaries while the OUT endpoints will be on even index boundaries. But this usb_dc_ep_check_cap() probably doesn't want to make this assumption and instead let the calling function, usb_validate_ep_cfg_data() sequentially set the index without concern about the even/odd.

But the problem is that the usb_dc_ep_check_cap() is checking a temporary address value and returning false because it knows it is an IN endpoint but the address is not odd. So it returns back to the calling function and increments to the next index value to check. The result is that you get a address value for the IN endpoint of 0x85 and later the macro EP_ABS_IDX() calculates the index value of the endpoint and gets 11 which is tested against NUM_OF_EP_MAX which is 8.

The simple "fix" is to not do these odd/even tests in usb_dc_ep_check_cap() but there is another layer to this problem. In cdc_acm.c, it ends up defining two instances of the `struct usb_ep_cfg_data` array (cdc_acm_ep_data_0 and cdc_acm_ep_data_1) where each of these have two IN endpoints and one OUT endpoint. I don't know enough about the underlying logic here but this results in four IN endpoints trying to be "fixed up" with the above routines so you have addresses 0x81-0x84. The macro that generates the index will now get a value of 9 for address 0x84 which fails the test against number of endpoints supported.

I don't know how these index values get mapped to the actual hardware but it looks like we are trying to have a logical index values as maintained by the USB stack (with >0x80 for IN endpoints) and have that mapped to the physical endpoints of the underlying hardware. 

The CDC-ACM appears to ultimately want to configure 4 IN and 2 OUT endpoints. The logic will map the IN endpoints to odd index values and not use all the available index value leaving a number of index values unused while at the same time failing the condition test on maximum number of endpoints.

Finally second patch below seems to fix the issue. I forgot again about this sub-shim layer in the mcux hal and that makes this driver unmaintainable. I need to look at it again in peace. I will open a PR to fix this bug.

```diff
diff --git a/mcux/middleware/usb/device/usb_device_ehci.h b/mcux/middleware/usb/device/usb_device_ehci.h
index 08b9700..a29a423 100644
--- a/mcux/middleware/usb/device/usb_device_ehci.h
+++ b/mcux/middleware/usb/device/usb_device_ehci.h
@@ -19,7 +19,7 @@
  * Definitions
  ******************************************************************************/
 
-#define USB_DEVICE_CONFIG_ENDPOINTS (DT_INST_PROP(0, num_bidir_endpoints) / 2)
+#define USB_DEVICE_CONFIG_ENDPOINTS (DT_INST_PROP(0, num_bidir_endpoints))
 
 /*! @brief The maximum value of ISO type maximum packet size for HS in USB specification 2.0 */
 #define USB_DEVICE_MAX_HS_ISO_MAX_PACKET_SIZE (1024U)
```

The relationship between the DTS, USB stack, and the kinetis/mcux/HAL enablement seems a bit convoluted. The DTS setting for num-bidir-endpoints is the description of the hardware capabilities. It looks like the USB upper layer stack relies on the lower layer enablement to provide an error if the upper layer attempts to establish too many endpoints. So I find it confusing and odd that the solution here seems to mix in a 2x multiply (and divide) around endpoint counts. I'm also not sure what is driving the architecture to use an odd index for IN endpoints and even index for OUT endpoints?

The root problem is coming from how this code fixes up the endpoint addresses and then tries to map these addresses to index values. These index values are still a bit "virtual" and not directly related to the num_bidir_endpoints because we seem to want to only allow half the endpoints to be allocated to IN and another half to OUT direction based on how things are being encoded. The change you are highlighting to define NUM_OF_EP_MAX to be 2x the DTS defined num-bidir-endpoints is a bit of a hack because now you have the false virtual value for the number of endpoints. With this change, I believe we could end up defining more than 8 endpoints and the system wouldn't catch it as an error.

So some direct questions:

- Why the odd/even distinction on the endpoints? Is that a real HW constraint?
- Making the change in the HAL to remove the Divide by 2 seems like it may have a propagation issue to consider. A quick search of the HAL code indicates that the underlying code then has places were it multiplies the define by 2 for work it is doing. And frankly, looking at this HAL code it does look like the SW is splitting the endpoints between IN and OUT.

@jfischer-phytec-iot, discussed some of this with our internal SDK folks. They confirmed that the HAL definition that does the /2 is wrong as you have pointed out. 

They also clarified to me that when our platform says it has 8 multi-directional endpoints that functionally means there are 8 IN and 8 OUT endpoints.

@jfischer-phytec-iot I have a PR in the NXP HAL to address the divide by 2. 

zephyrproject-rtos/hal_nxp#54
@dleach02 Sorry for delay, I have opened #27824 and also placed explanation in the commit message.

review_comments:
I understand what you are doing here. One observation is that this NUM_OF_EP_MAX is the total number of endpoints but each endpoint is not equal. As long as the reader of the code understands that, at least in this case, this is the total count with an equal split between IN and OUT endpoints.

I also think that your comments in the commit should be pulled into the source code somewhere for the viewer to see and understand.
